title: Optic disc drusen and scleral canal size – protocol for a systematic review and meta-analysis
article_subtype: Protocol for a systematic review and meta-analysis
condition_or_topic: Optic disc drusen (ODD) and their relationship to scleral canal size
clinical_background: ODD are acellular deposits in the optic nerve head. Reported adult prevalence ranges from 0.2% to around 2.0%, while 0.4% of children are thought to be affected. Diagnosis is often incidental, but more than half of affected patients have visual field deficits, and a small number with large ODD develop severe complications. A narrow optic disc and scleral canal have been proposed as contributors to disrupted axoplasmic flow and ODD formation, although studies testing this hypothesis have reported divergent findings. Patient age, drusen location and measurement technique may influence the observed association. Measurements at the Bruch’s membrane opening (BMO) are commonly used as a proxy for the anterior scleral canal opening.
objectives: Determine the mean difference in scleral canal size at the level of the BMO between patients with ODD and healthy controls using fundus pictures.
Determine the mean difference in scleral canal size at the level of the BMO between patients with ODD and healthy controls using OCT (SD-EDI or SS).
In a subgroup analysis, determine the mean difference in scleral canal size at the level of the BMO between patients with buried ODD and patients with visible ODD using fundus pictures.
In a subgroup analysis, determine the mean difference in scleral canal size at the level of the BMO between patients with buried ODD and patients with visible ODD using OCT (SD-EDI or SS).
clinical_question: Patients: people with ODD, including those with buried or visible ODD. Intervention/exposure: scleral canal size measured at the level of the BMO using fundus pictures or OCT (SD-EDI or SS); no intervention is proposed. Comparators: healthy controls for the main comparisons and patients with visible ODD for the buried-ODD subgroup comparisons. Outcome: mean difference in scleral canal size between the respective groups.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: Earlier studies of the relationship between optic disc drusen (ODD) and scleral canal size have produced conflicting findings. The authors describe observations consistent with a role for a narrow canal, including small optic discs in affected families and smaller scleral canals in Usher syndrome than in other dystrophies. They also discuss a proposed vascular explanation for ODD formation, while noting that vascular abnormalities could instead result from constraints imposed by a narrow canal. The planned review has no results with which to resolve these explanations.
clinical_implications: Identifying factors involved in ODD development could help identify patients at risk, improve screening and follow-up, and potentially enable earlier care before severe complications occur.

If the review supports an association between narrow scleral canals and ODD, canal size could help define a population for studies of other potential risk factors or preventive treatments. The authors do not know of a way to enlarge the scleral canal and therefore do not regard it as a modifiable risk factor.
limitations: Following PRISMA methods cannot fully overcome limitations in the studies that will be included.
The authors anticipate moderate to high heterogeneity related to factors such as patient age, measurement methods and magnification correction.
open_questions: Whether a narrow scleral canal is associated with ODD remains unresolved.
It remains unclear how much of the differing findings across studies may be explained by differences between buried and visible ODD.
The authors cannot predict the effect of widening the scleral canal.
The potential value of lowering intra-ocular pressure remains under consideration; whether neuroprotective treatments could halt progressive atrophy in patients with ODD is also uncertain.
future_directions: The planned review will examine the association between scleral canal size and ODD, with a subgroup analysis of buried versus visible ODD to explore possible sources of heterogeneity.
If an association is supported, the findings could help define a population for studies testing modification of other potential risk factors or preventive treatments.
study_design: Protocol for a systematic review and meta-analysis of studies comparing scleral canal size in patients with optic disc drusen (ODD) and healthy subjects, with a planned subgroup comparison of buried and visible ODD. Eligible designs include randomized and non-randomized controlled trials and observational studies. Searches will cover articles published before November 29, 2022 in MEDLINE via PubMed, Cochrane and EMBASE, as well as grey literature, trial registers and reference lists. The review will follow PRISMA and MOOSE guidance.

population.description: Patients with clinically or imaging-diagnosed ODD and healthy subjects; the subgroup analysis will compare patients with buried ODD against those with visible ODD.
inclusion_criteria: Randomized controlled trials, non-randomized controlled trials and observational studies.
ODD diagnosed clinically or by imaging with autofluorescence, B-scan ultrasound, OCT or CT scan.
Studies quantifying scleral canal size and providing a relevant control group: healthy subjects for the ODD comparison or patients with visible ODD for the buried ODD comparison.
exclusion_criteria: Reviews, meta-analyses, follow-up studies using previously published data and case reports.
Studies without participants with ODD, a quantified scleral canal size or the relevant control group.
Studies limited to syndromic ODD, including ODD associated with Pseudoxanthoma Elasticum, Retinitis Pigmentosa, Usher syndrome, Down Syndrome, Alagille Syndrome or Noonan syndrome.

Studies using time-domain OCT (TD-OCT) or non-EDI SD OCT to measure scleral canal size at the BMO will be excluded from the meta-analysis but retained for the systematic review and sensitivity analysis.
For OCT-based comparisons, studies that do not use EDI SD OCT or SS OCT to exclude ODD and define a normal optic nerve according to the Copenhagen Consortium will not be included.
Articles without sufficient data to pool outcomes after the authors have been contacted for missing material.

comparators: Healthy subjects compared with patients with ODD.
Patients with visible ODD compared with patients with buried ODD.

primary: Mean difference in scleral canal size at the BMO between patients with ODD and healthy controls, assessed using fundus pictures.
Mean difference in scleral canal size at the BMO between patients with ODD and healthy controls, assessed using OCT (SD-EDI or SS).
secondary: Mean difference in scleral canal size at the BMO between patients with buried ODD and patients with visible ODD, assessed using fundus pictures.
Mean difference in scleral canal size at the BMO between patients with buried ODD and patients with visible ODD, assessed using OCT (SD-EDI or SS).

statistical_methods: Extracted study data will be described and pooled as Hedge’s standardized mean difference, following the Cochrane Collaboration handbook. When necessary, reported optic disc measurements will be converted to mean diameter. Means and standard deviations will be extracted when available; estimates based on medians and quartiles will use the stated distributional assumptions or the methods of Luo et al. and Shi et al. Graph-only values will be extracted independently by two assessors with Plot Digitizer and averaged. A fixed-effects model is planned for I2< 50%, and a random-effects model otherwise; a 95% confidence interval excluding the null value will be considered significant. Between-study variance, t2, will be estimated by Restricted Maximum-Likelihood. Publication bias will be examined with Egger’s statistical test and funnel-plot inspection. Sensitivity analyses will restrict the synthesis to studies that computed mean diameter and, separately, add studies using TD-OCT or non-EDI SD OCT. Analyses and plots will use R v4.0.3 with the ‘Metafor’ package.
quality_assessment_tool: A domain-based grid adapted from the National Institutes of Health quality assessment tool of case-control studies will assess included studies. GRADE will assess evidence quality for each outcome if enough RCTs and interventional studies are included.
main_conclusion: This article presents a protocol, not completed findings. The planned review and meta-analysis aims to clarify whether scleral canal size differs between patients with optic disc drusen and healthy controls, and whether it differs between buried and visible drusen. The authors suggest that evidence for an association could help identify patients for future studies of other potential risk factors or preventive approaches.
narrative_summary:
Optic disc drusen (ODD) can be associated with visual field loss and, in a small number of patients, serious vascular complications. The authors examine a longstanding but disputed hypothesis: that a narrow scleral canal contributes to ODD formation. This article is a protocol, so it reports no pooled estimates or clinical findings from the proposed review.

The planned systematic review will search published studies dated before November 29, 2022, as well as grey literature. It will compare scleral canal size at the level of the Bruch’s membrane opening in patients with ODD and healthy controls, using measurements from fundus images or OCT. A subgroup analysis will compare buried with visible ODD. Eligible studies must provide a relevant comparison group and sufficient measurement data for analysis. The authors plan to assess study quality, examine heterogeneity and publication bias, and conduct sensitivity analyses concerning measurement methods.

For clinical practice, the review may help clarify whether canal size is associated with ODD, but it cannot yet establish that association. The authors anticipate heterogeneity related to age and measurement methods, among other factors. They also state that they know of no way to enlarge the scleral canal; if an association is supported, its value may instead lie in defining populations for research on other potential risk factors or preventive treatments.

document_sections.heading: Background
document_sections.content: Around one in forty patients receive a diagnosis of optic disc drusen (ODD) during their lifetime. These acellular deposits can have consequences ranging from asymptomatic visual field loss to arterial occlusion and subsequent blindness. Their origin remains disputed. A hypothesis proposed 50 years ago holds that a narrow optic disc and scleral canal disrupt axoplasmic transport and thereby promote ODD formation; this remains contested. The planned systematic review and meta-analysis will compare scleral canal size in people with ODD and healthy subjects to assess that hypothesis.

document_sections.heading: Methods
document_sections.content: The authors plan to search MEDLINE via PubMed, Cochrane, EMBASE, and grey literature for articles published before November 29, 2022 that measure scleral canal size in patients with ODD and healthy subjects. Eligible studies will include people with clinically or imaging-diagnosed ODD and healthy subjects. A subgroup analysis will compare buried ODD with visible ODD. Extracted study data will be described, and effect sizes will be calculated according to the Cochrane Collaboration handbook.

document_sections.heading: Discussion
document_sections.content: Whether a narrow scleral canal increases the risk of ODD remains unresolved. The planned synthesis may help clarify the competing interpretations. Better identification of factors involved in ODD development could help identify patients at risk and inform approaches to preventing advanced disease. Studying people with small scleral canals could also reveal associated factors and improve understanding of the condition.

document_sections.heading: Systematic review registration
document_sections.content: The planned review is registered at https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero/display_ record.php?ID=CRD42022375110.

document_sections.heading: 1 Introduction
document_sections.content: ODD are acellular accumulations thought to arise from axonal breakdown after disruption of axoplasmic transport in the optic nerve head. Reported adult prevalence ranges from 0.2% to around 2.0%; an estimated 0.4% of children are affected. Diagnosis is often incidental, either in children investigated for pseudo-papilloedema or in adults whose drusen are visible at the disc margin. More than half of patients have visual field deficits, including enlargement of the blind spot or field constriction, associated with retinal nerve fiber layer atrophy. A small number of patients with large ODD develop serious complications, including choroidal neovascularization, central artery occlusion, or anterior ischemic neuropathy. Identifying risk factors might support screening and more targeted follow-up of ODD and its consequences. A longstanding proposal is that a narrow scleral canal creates greater mechanical stress on axons and favors ODD formation, but studies testing this proposal have produced divergent findings. Drusen location, patient age, and measurement instrument may affect results, motivating a systematic assessment of the relationship between ODD and optic disc and scleral canal size. The anterior opening of the optic nerve scleral canal is the anatomical entrance at the scleral level. Its dimensions are commonly assessed from fundus photographs, using disc boundaries, or with optical coherence tomography (OCT). Many studies use Bruch’s membrane opening (BMO) dimensions as a proxy for dimensions at the anterior scleral canal opening. BMO is clearly delineated on OCT and appears stable across time and conditions. High-resolution enhanced depth imaging spectral-domain OCT (EDI SD-OCT) and swept source OCT (SS-OCT) penetrate more deeply and characterize deep structures better, with fewer drusen-related artifacts. The Optic Disc Drusen Studies Consortium recommends EDI-SD-OCT with scan averaging for ODD diagnosis; it has been found equivalent to SS-OCT for that purpose. The review will assess the mean difference in scleral canal size at BMO between patients with ODD and healthy controls, separately for measurements from fundus photographs and from OCT (SD-EDI or SS). It will also examine mean differences using each measurement approach between buried and visible ODD.

document_sections.heading: 2 Methods/design
document_sections.content: The planned literature search and analysis will follow Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) and Meta-analysis of Observational Studies in Epidemiology (MOOSE) guidance.

document_sections.heading: 2.1 Search strategy
document_sections.content: MEDLINE via PubMed, Cochrane, and EMBASE will be searched for articles published before November 29, 2022 that compare mean scleral canal size at BMO between ODD and healthy controls or between buried and visible ODD. Grey literature searches will cover Google Scholar, Greylit.org, World Health Organization Clinical Trials Search Portal, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the European Union Clinical Trials Register. Reference lists and bibliographies of included studies will be checked for additional eligible work. The planned MeSH search combines optic AND (disk OR disc OR nerve) AND drusen AND (canal OR area OR size OR measure OR crowded OR small).

document_sections.heading: 2.2 Inclusion criteria
document_sections.content: Randomized controlled trials, non-randomized controlled trials, and observational studies will be eligible. Patients must have an ODD diagnosis established clinically or by imaging, including autofluorescence, B-scan ultrasound, OCT, or CT scan.

document_sections.heading: 2.3 Exclusion criteria
document_sections.content: Reviews, meta-analyses, follow-up studies presenting previously published data, and case reports will be excluded. Studies will also be excluded if they lack people with ODD, do not quantify scleral canal size, or lack the relevant control group: healthy subjects for an ODD comparison or patients with visible ODD for a buried ODD comparison. Studies restricted to syndromic ODD will be excluded; examples of associated predisposing syndromes are Pseudoxanthoma Elasticum, Retinitis Pigmentosa, Usher syndrome, Down Syndrome, Alagille Syndrome, and Noonan syndrome. Studies measuring BMO-level canal size with time-domain OCT (TD-OCT) or non-EDI SD OCT will be excluded from the primary meta-analysis but retained for the systematic review and sensitivity analysis. For the OCT-based main objective and subgroup analysis, eligibility also requires EDI SD OCT or SS OCT to exclude ODD and define a normal optic nerve according to the Copenhagen Consortium. An article will be excluded from pooling if adequate data remain unavailable after its authors have been contacted. Data will suffice if both groups have sample sizes, means, and standard deviations; sample sizes, medians, and all four quartiles; or individual raw values.

document_sections.heading: 2.5 Risk of bias appraisal
document_sections.content: Study quality will be evaluated with a domain-based grid adapted from the National Institutes of Health quality assessment tool for case-control studies. AVJ and MR will assess studies independently without seeing each other’s scores, then discuss disagreements; DBG will adjudicate if they cannot agree. Potential publication bias will be examined with Egger’s statistical test and visual assessment of a funnel plot displaying estimated effect size against its standard error mean. An asymmetric inverted funnel would favor publication bias.

document_sections.heading: 2.6.1 Study review
document_sections.content: After study selection, references will be entered into Microsoft® Excel (version 16.65) for extraction. AVJ will extract and collate information, and MR will verify the material from every included article. Extracted study details will include authors, title, publication year, eligibility criteria, and sample size. Population details will include the proportion with buried versus visible drusen, age, and spheric equivalent. Outcome details will include the parameter measured, means and standard deviations or median and interquartile range (IQR), OCT type when relevant, and any magnification-correction formula. Statistical details will include normality testing, tests applied, correction for multiple comparisons, confounders, and parameter significance. Extraction tables will be piloted and refined. Means and standard deviations will be taken directly when reported. For medians and IQR, the authors will check available protocols and methods to determine whether reporting reflects skewed data or author preference without normality testing despite a sufficiently large sample. If the choice is unexplained and sample size is above 50, they will assume a normal distribution and use the stated transformation, mean = median and SD = 1IQR:35. Otherwise, they plan to use the formulas attributed to Luo et al. and Shi et al. for estimating the mean and standard deviation from reported summary values; the printed expressions include w1 = 2:2+2:n20:75 and w2 = 0:7 − n00:72:55, but the equations are not fully legible in the article. The article identifies a as the minimum, q1 as the first quartile, q3 as the third quartile, b as the maximum, and f−1(z) as the upper zth percentile of the standard normal distribution. If suitable summaries are absent, raw values will be sought. If still unavailable, the corresponding author will be contacted up to three times by e-mail; a study lacking the necessary information will be excluded from meta-analysis. Missing main-text data will also be sought in supplementary materials. If results appear only in graphs, AVJ and MR will each extract values with Plot Digitizer, and their mean will be used.

document_sections.heading: 2.4 Review process
document_sections.content: The article includes a PRISMA flow chart outlining the planned review. AVJ will screen potentially eligible studies. Articles will be imported into Zotero and assessed by title, abstract, and, when necessary, full text to remove those that fail eligibility criteria. Data will then be extracted from included papers, which will also undergo risk-of-bias assessment.

document_sections.heading: 2.6.2 Strategy for data synthesis
document_sections.content: Data from included articles will be described, and effect sizes will be calculated in line with the Cochrane Collaboration handbook using Cochrane Review Manager v5.3. A preliminary search indicates that mean diameter and total area are common descriptors of optic disc size. The authors will report only mean diameter because its calculation is more straightforward. Where necessary, they plan to derive it from reported maximum and minimum diameters, horizontal diameter, or total area, assuming the optic disc can be approximated by a disc. The printed diameter expressions are partly unclear; the horizontal-diameter rule states that mean diameter equals horizontal diameter, while the total-area expression begins with 2. Data will be pooled as Hedge’s standardized mean difference. A fixed-effects model will be used for low-to-moderate heterogeneity (I2< 50%); otherwise, a random-effects model will be applied. A 95% confidence interval excluding the null value will indicate significance. Between-study variance, t2, will be estimated with the Restricted Maximum-Likelihood formula. Statistical analyses and plots will use R v4.0.3 and the ‘Metafor’ package.

document_sections.heading: 2.6.3 Sensitivity analysis
document_sections.content: Two sensitivity analyses are planned. To assess the assumption that the optic disc can be approximated by a disc, one analysis will retain only studies that calculated mean diameter. To assess the restriction to recent OCT modalities, the other will add studies using TD-OCT or non-EDI SD OCT. Both will be reported in a summary table. If enough RCTs and interventional studies are included, evidence quality for each outcome will be assessed with GRADE criteria following Cochrane Collaboration recommendations.

document_sections.heading: 3 Discussion
document_sections.content: Identifying causes of ODD might improve screening and, through earlier diagnosis and care, help prevent severe complications. The authors know of no way to enlarge the scleral canal and therefore do not regard canal size as a modifiable risk factor; they also cannot predict the effects of widening it. If the planned study supports an association between a narrow canal and ODD, it could help define a population for studies of other potentially modifiable risks or preventive treatments. The possible value of reducing intra-ocular pressure remains under consideration, while neuroprotective treatments under development might help arrest progressive atrophy in ODD. Several previously reported observations support the narrow-canal hypothesis. Genetic contributions have been proposed with an irregular autosomal dominant pattern, and affected families have been observed to have small optic discs. ODD occur mainly in caucasians, whose optic discs are smaller than those of African and Asian people. ODD are more frequent in rod-cone dystrophies, particularly Usher syndrome, for which smaller scleral canals than in other dystrophies have been reported. In healthy subjects, optic disc size correlates with axial length; reports also indicate that ODD prevalence is higher in nanophtalmos and posterior microphthalmos than in the general population, and that ODD presence correlates with axial length in nanophtalmos. Pseudoxanthoma elasticum is associated with ODD, although the authors know of no demonstrated direct connection to scleral canal size. They speculate that mineralization and resulting rigidity of Bruch’s membrane in this condition might increase stress on nerve fibers at its opening. An alternative proposed explanation links ODD to abnormal vascular anatomy and branching: higher frequencies of trifurcation and cilioretinal arteries have been observed in patients with ODD. Under that proposal, abnormal permeability and an impaired blood barrier cause chronic ischemia and calcium accumulation, leading to ODD. A reported association between small scleral canals and vascular anomalies in ODD leaves open the possibility that abnormal vessels instead result from greater constraints imposed by a narrow canal before and after birth. The authors acknowledge that following PRISMA cannot fully compensate for limitations of included studies. They anticipate moderate to high heterogeneity from differences including age, measurement methods, and magnification correction. These factors will be addressed in the narrative review. The buried-versus-visible ODD subgroup analysis might explain some heterogeneity and conflicting findings. Grey literature will be searched alongside published literature to reduce the file-drawer problem and associated publication bias.
